## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Tindukajātaka* (Ja 177) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection, positioned in Fausböll's edition within the second *nipāta* between the *Kalāyamutthijātaka* and the *Kacchapajātaka* [Fausböll 1879]. The frame narrative is set at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, where the Buddha delivers the discourse on the subject of the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*) [Fausböll 1879]. Having heard praise of his own discernment, he observes that he was fertile in resource and wise in former lives as well, drawing a comparison to the *Mahābodhijātaka* and the *Ummaggajātaka* [Fausböll 1879].

The verse opens with the incipit *Dhanuhatthakalāpehīti* ("All around us see them stand") [Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, a troop of monkeys ventures into a human settlement at night to gather the fruit of a *tinduka* tree [UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. When the villagers discover them and surround the tree, the monkey troop avoids slaughter through tactical ingenuity: a fire is set to the village upwind, causing the villagers to abandon the cordon to quench the blaze, thereby enabling the monkeys to escape with their fruit [UNDV Conference Volume 2009; Fausböll 1879]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha identifies the chief of the monkeys (*vānarinda*) as himself, the nephew Senaka as the Sakyan Mahānāma, and the monkey troop as the Buddha's present assembly [Fausböll 1879].
